title: From dummy to professional: LLMs and models
audience: Experienced systems programmer, new to machine learning
language: Python for minimal executable examples; C/C++/Metal and memory-layout parallels; optional Rust translations
scope_note: Professional competence is demonstrated by artifacts and independent reviews, not promised by finishing a fixed number of hours. These are planned episodes, not completed course content.

chapters.title: A map of learned software
chapters.goal: Locate data, code, parameters, inference and training in one system.
episodes: A model is a parameterized program
Training versus inference versus fine-tuning
From text to token IDs and predictions
TAH, IOTA, SN9 and our four Macs: the map
chapters.lab: Trace one text example through a tiny prediction program; distinguish code from learned parameters.
chapters.check: Explain which state changes during inference, backward and an optimizer step; identify training versus serving logs.
chapters.misconception: A model contains a database of all its training examples or learns automatically from every prompt.

chapters.title: Tensors are structured buffers
chapters.goal: Reason about shape, dtype, layout and memory before using a framework.
episodes: Scalars, vectors, matrices and tensor shapes
Strides, views, broadcasting and aliasing
Dot products, matrix multiplication and reductions
FP32, FP16, BF16 and why order matters
chapters.lab: Manipulate a tensor memory viewer; reconstruct offsets and expose a wrong transpose.
chapters.check: Predict output shapes and allocation sizes; explain a finite but wrong result.
chapters.misconception: A view is always a copy, or identical formulas imply identical floating-point results.

chapters.title: What learning actually optimizes
chapters.goal: Compute a loss and explain why an update can improve it.
episodes: One weight, one prediction, one loss
Derivatives as sensitivity; the chain rule
Gradient descent and learning rate
Batches, train/validation/test and generalization
chapters.lab: Adjust a scalar model, compute its slope, and see understepping and overshooting.
chapters.check: Compute one update by hand and distinguish training loss from unseen-data performance.
chapters.misconception: Lower training loss always means a better model, or the gradient points downhill.

chapters.title: Forward, backward, update
chapters.goal: Implement and test reverse-mode automatic differentiation.
episodes: Forward builds values and a computation graph
Backward propagates sensitivities
Saved activations, recomputation and gradient accumulation
Build a tiny autodiff engine
chapters.lab: Capstone A: scalar reverse-mode engine with shared nodes, fan-out and gradient checks.
chapters.check: Predict every gradient and weight before/after backward and optimizer.step; fix missing accumulation.
chapters.misconception: Backward changes the weights, or simply runs the forward code in reverse.

chapters.title: From neurons to a training loop
chapters.goal: Train and debug a small network with the same conceptual pieces as a large one.
episodes: Linear layers, nonlinearity and composition
Initialization, normalization and residual paths
SGD, momentum, AdamW and optimizer state
Checkpoints, reproducibility and broken training loops
chapters.lab: Train a tiny MLP and diagnose wrong-sign updates, stale gradients and optimizer state mismatch.
chapters.check: Explain each line of a training loop and account for parameters, gradients and optimizer memory.
chapters.misconception: The checkpoint is only the weights, or optimizer state is interchangeable across runs.

chapters.title: How language models work
chapters.goal: Explain next-token training and construct the data/loss path.
episodes: Tokenization, embeddings and positional information
Logits, softmax and cross-entropy
Teacher forcing, causal masking and sequence batches
Sampling, context, KV caches and inference costs
chapters.lab: Inspect logits and probabilities in a small vocabulary and compute a next-token loss.
chapters.check: Detect target leakage, shifted-label bugs and confusion between training and inference caches.
chapters.misconception: Loss is accuracy, attention sees future tokens, or a token is always a word.

chapters.title: Inside a transformer
chapters.goal: Trace shapes and gradients through a transformer block.
episodes: Queries, keys and values as learned projections
Attention scores, masking, softmax and weighted values
Heads, grouped-query attention, RoPE and RMSNorm
Assemble and train a tiny decoder
chapters.lab: Capstone B: small CPU transformer; inspect attention and compare gradients to a reference.
chapters.check: Trace Q/K/V and projection dimensions; show how an incorrect output can corrupt upstream gradients.
chapters.misconception: An attention head is a TAH layer, or attention weights alone fully explain a model.

chapters.title: The software stack under Python
chapters.goal: Read a framework operation down to its device implementation.
episodes: PyTorch tensors, modules, autograd and optimizers
Dispatch, operator implementations and asynchronous devices
MLX: arrays, lazy evaluation, transforms and memory
Training, fine-tuning, LoRA, evaluation and alignment
chapters.lab: Implement the same small operation in plain Python and PyTorch; compare an optional MLX variant.
chapters.check: Explain framework versus backend versus kernel, and why framework replacement requires qualification.
chapters.misconception: MLX is a PyTorch flag, or pretraining creates a finished instruction-following assistant.

chapters.title: What the GPU actually does
chapters.goal: Relate ML operations to parallel execution, data movement and synchronization.
episodes: Threads, SIMD groups, threadgroups and parallel reductions
Memory hierarchy, tiling, occupancy and arithmetic intensity
Metal, MPS, MPSGraph, TensorOps and GPU neural accelerators
Why Apple silicon fits this use case—and its limits
chapters.lab: A tiled matrix multiplication simulator with bytes moved, FLOPs and a scheduling timeline.
chapters.check: Choose between fusion, tiling and reducing transfers from a profile; distinguish GPU accelerators from ANE.
chapters.misconception: Unified memory is free memory, GPU utilization equals useful work, or all Macs are faster than datacenter GPUs.

chapters.title: One model across many machines
chapters.goal: Trace a distributed training sample and its return gradients.
episodes: Data, tensor and pipeline parallelism
Microbatches, bubbles, stale work and backpressure
IOTA orchestration, peer routing and replicated splits
Upload, pseudo-gradients, merge and the next epoch
chapters.lab: Pause a simulated peer and inspect queued activations, deadlines and accepted completions.
chapters.check: Route a forward and backward through L0/L1/L2; explain local updates versus global merge.
chapters.misconception: Our four Macs form a fixed private pipeline, or a TAH epoch necessarily means one pass over the dataset.

chapters.title: Read the actual TAH worker
chapters.goal: Connect the mental model to versioned code and observed events.
episodes: Official host, worker process and control plane
Head/body/tail split implementations
Training queue, activation cache and optimizer boundary
Our behavioral patches, telemetry and admission lifecycle
chapters.lab: Follow an anonymized recorded sample through pinned source and journal events.
chapters.check: Identify where a sample waited versus computed; explain why local backward completion does not prove credited work.
chapters.misconception: The GUI performs tensor math, or a worker registered in a run is necessarily training.

chapters.title: The corruption incident
chapters.goal: Reconstruct a numerical failure from evidence and design a stronger test.
episodes: Finite, deterministic and correct are different claims
The M5 coordinate-layout bug and forward/backward damage
Batch calibration, fallback changes and misleading smoke tests
Diagnosis, containment, disclosure and causal uncertainty
chapters.lab: Replay a tiny analogous layout bug; compare forward, dQ, dK and dV and assemble an evidence timeline.
chapters.check: Reject a finite-only test, design chip-specific counterexamples, and separate measured causality from historical inference.
chapters.misconception: Passing on one chip qualifies another, or a healthy run-loss plot proves local equivalence.

chapters.title: Optimize without changing the answer
chapters.goal: Design a measured, numerically justified optimization and its rollback.
episodes: Head/loss tiling and finite-check synchronization
Normalization fusion, recomputation and buffer lifetime
Attention layouts, precision and forward/backward qualification
Benchmarking, memory gates, fault injection and guarded rollout
chapters.lab: Capstone C: qualify a small kernel-like transformation against independent reference and negative controls.
chapters.check: Catch a misleading microbenchmark, invalid comparison, retained buffer and false-success guard.
chapters.misconception: A faster isolated kernel guarantees higher tokens/hour, or a passing old artifact qualifies edited source.

chapters.title: Operate like an ML systems engineer
chapters.goal: Defend an end-to-end design and communicate the limits of its evidence.
episodes: Read papers, distinguish claims and inspect implementations
Build a reproducible experiment and evidence report
End-to-end performance, network limits and resource budgets
Final review: teach back, diagnose and propose a safe improvement
chapters.lab: Final portfolio: tiny model, gradient tests, distributed trace, incident reconstruction, benchmark and rollout proposal.
chapters.check: Independent oral/written defense plus a new held-out debugging task and delayed revisit.
chapters.misconception: Course completion is equivalent to professional certification or proof of production safety.

suggested_paths.orientation: A 2–3 hour guided map drawn from chapters 1, 4, 9, 10 and 12; explicitly does not confer mastery.
suggested_paths.core: 56 episodes, typically 12–20 minutes of focused explanation/practice; labs and reviews extend the planned total to roughly 35–50 learner hours. Re-estimate after pilot.
suggested_paths.deep: Optional tensor algebra, Metal/C++ kernel, framework source and distributed consistency branches; roughly 60–90 total hours including larger capstones, depending on diagnostic results. No fixed expertise promise.

policy_requirement: Every enrollment must resolve a bounded policy or explicitly permitted open-ended mode. POC deadline/duration and extension amounts are to be configured, not silently assigned by the design.
administration: Course core provides the same scoped admin interface for this private module as for every other SDK course.
delivery: One guided path with explicit readiness gates; contextual optional help; reviewed/generated media and conversational or interactive evidence.
platform_requirement: Required learning objectives supported on iOS/iPadOS, Android phones/tablets, mobile web and widescreen web; platform adapters or objective-equivalent fallbacks validated.
placement: Admin-enabled and learner-optional. Author a concept-mapped blueprint before granting exemptions; placement is not fabricated lesson completion or retained mastery.
